We’re excited to share a major milestone in the formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture.

https://projectnumina.ai/article?slug=Kakeya

At Project Numina, we formalized the proof of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture in Lean from the Sticky Kakeya theorem, following the streamlined argument of Guth, Wang and Zahl.

A crucial part of the story comes from Nankai University and the ByteDance Seed AI4Math Team. Their project provides a sorry-free, unconditional formalization of Wang–Zahl Theorem 5.2, the Sticky Kakeya result that our development takes as its main input:

https://github.com/M32026/3d-sticky-kakeya

The scale of this contribution is substantial. Early in our project, we deliberately treated Sticky Kakeya as an external input because we estimated that formalizing it could require around five times as much additional work as the rest of the argument we were undertaking.

Our development is here:

https://github.com/project-numina/kakeya-3d

Together, the two developments give an unconditional formal proof of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, with no sorry and no project-specific mathematical axiom.

More broadly, this project is an experiment in how AI can help turn frontier mathematics into machine-verified proofs. The final result is genuinely collaborative, combining the mathematical work of Guth, Wang and Zahl with the crucial Sticky Kakeya formalization by Nankai University × ByteDance Seed AI4Math.

Limitations and what comes next

Much of the code was AI-generated. While the proof checks formally, the code is far from being at Mathlib quality. We’re committed to supporting the long-term refactoring effort and upstreaming the most important reusable lemmas and infrastructure.

AI is rapidly changing how mathematics is done. Numina wants to explore that transition in the open and help build an open ecosystem around AI-assisted mathematics. We hope more mathematicians and formalizers will join the discussion and help shape what comes next.

@Junqi Liu @Zheng Yuan @Bolton Bailey @Justin Asher

we deliberately treated Sticky Kakeya as an external input because we estimated that formalizing it could require around five times as much additional work as the rest of the argument we were undertaking.

This estimate is quite accurate, as the ratio turned out to be 1829417/413533=4.42x lines of Lean files.

Worth highlighting from the blog post:

The paper states that such a family can be extracted by repeated pigeonholing, with losses small enough for the later estimates. Proving this refinement became one of our most time-consuming tasks. After many attempts, we found, with AI’s help, a counterexample to our literal implementation of the definition.
